objective.statement: Name the degrees of a scale by their technical names.
successCriteria: I know the seven names from tonic to leading note.
I can name a given note's degree in a key.
I can find the note that has a given technical name.

explanation.text: Besides numbers, each note of a major or minor scale has a technical name. In order they are: tonic (1st), supertonic (2nd), mediant (3rd), subdominant (4th), dominant (5th), submediant (6th) and leading note (7th). The octave is the (upper) tonic.

The names tell a story. The tonic is the keynote. The dominant, the 5th degree, 'dominates' the tonic with its strong pull towards it. The leading note is a semitone below the tonic and 'leads' to it, so it is always the raised 7th: in a minor key, the harmonic minor raises it to make a leading note.

The supertonic is the note above the tonic. The mediant is halfway between the tonic and the dominant. The subdominant is as far below the tonic as the dominant is above it, and the submediant is as far below the tonic as the mediant is above it.

steps: B is the tonic, the 1st note. C♯ is the supertonic.
D♯ is the mediant, E the subdominant, F♯ the dominant.
G♯ is the submediant and A♯ the leading note, a semitone below the top B.

mastery.completion: The lesson is complete when every step has been answered correctly (retries allowed). Only first-attempt, hint-free independent answers count as mastery evidence; guided steps never do.

provenance.authoredBy: Music Theory Path curriculum team (Brief 05, drafted with AI assistance; pending qualified teacher review)
provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 11 and First Steps Grade 4 section 8 (pp. 86-88): the seven technical names and their meaning. The book explains the leading note as always the major 7th, so minor questions use the harmonic minor and say so. 'Subtonic' (the lowered 7th) is not taught or asked.
